title: Bangladesh measles deaths pass 1,370 as WHO flags risk at Bengal border crossings
dek: More than 2.6 lakh suspected cases have been reported since March, most in children under five, after a vaccine stockout. WHO rates the regional risk as high and names crossings opposite North 24 Parganas and Malda.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh's measles outbreak has now been linked to 1,371 deaths this year, according to figures from the country's Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), the country's deadliest measles outbreak in decades, according to reports. Eight more deaths, one confirmed and seven suspected, were reported in the 24 hours to 8 am on Thursday, along with 1,007 new suspected cases.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has rated the risk of the outbreak as high both for Bangladesh and for the South-East Asia region, and has warned that busy land crossings from high-incidence districts into India raise the chance of the virus being carried across the border into West Bengal.

## The numbers

According to the DGHS figures, reported on Thursday:

- 1,371 deaths this year: 106 confirmed as measles and 1,265 suspected
- 2,61,535 suspected cases, of which 26,476 have been confirmed in laboratories
- 2,34,280 suspected patients admitted to hospital since 15 March, of whom 2,25,268 have recovered

Most of the deaths are recorded as suspected rather than confirmed, which means they occurred in patients with measles symptoms who were not tested. The figures are the government's own and have not been independently verified.

The outbreak has grown sharply since WHO was first notified on 4 April. In its disease outbreak notice of 23 April, WHO counted 19,161 suspected cases and 166 suspected deaths between 15 March and 14 April, in 58 of the country's 64 districts. In that period 79% of cases were in children under five, 66% under two, and a third were infants younger than nine months, too young for their first dose.

## Why it happened

WHO said the outbreak followed a nationwide stockout of measles-rubella (MR) vaccine in 2024 and 2025, which cut routine coverage, and the absence of any regular nationwide catch-up campaign since 2020. Many of the children who fell ill had never been vaccinated or had received only one of the two doses, UNICEF found.

The government, with UNICEF, WHO and the vaccine alliance Gavi, began an emergency MR campaign on 5 April in 30 sub-districts of 18 high-risk districts and extended it nationwide on 20 April, for children aged six months to five years. More than 1.66 lakh children were vaccinated in the Rohingya camps in Cox's Bazar. Vitamin A is being given to all suspected and confirmed patients.

Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known. Two doses of vaccine give about 97% protection, and WHO says at least 95% of children in every area need both doses to stop it spreading.

## What it means for India and Bengal

WHO named Jashore and Chapainawabganj, districts with high incidence, as having busy land crossings into India. Jashore lies opposite the Petrapole-Benapole crossing in North 24 Parganas, the busiest land port between the two countries, and Chapainawabganj borders Malda. WHO also noted that India had reported a rise in measles cases over the previous six months despite high vaccination coverage. It recommends stronger surveillance in high-traffic border areas, rapid response teams for imported cases, isolation in hospitals and vaccination of health and transport workers, but says it does not recommend any restriction on travel or trade.

India's national coverage is high: 98% of children received a first dose and 95% a second in 2025, according to WHO and UNICEF estimates cited in reports. National averages can hide local pockets of low coverage. A measles outbreak of five cases in Jhargram district this year was listed as under control in the national disease surveillance programme's weekly report. The West Bengal health department has not announced any special measures for border districts.

## What happens next

The DGHS publishes daily figures. With new suspected cases still running at about 1,000 a day, health agencies are pressing for a further round of vaccination and for routine immunisation to be restored in full, while WHO has asked neighbouring countries to watch for imported cases.
